Gold made a seven-week high on Thursday, and the metal that carried it there stopped.

At 6:03am New York, Kitco had gold bid $4,270.90, up 0.58% and a fourth consecutive session higher. Platinum $1,753.00, up 1.33%. Palladium $1,367.00, up 1.48%. Silver $61.67, down 0.41% — the only one of the four in the red, after leading the complex all week with gains of 3.27% and 3.2%.

For the bench the number is the gram. Fine gold is $137.31 a gram against $133.68 on Wednesday and $130.17 on Tuesday: $7.14 added to the metal cost of every piece in your case in two days. The gold to silver ratio widened back to 69.3 from 67.8, undoing two sessions of tightening in one.

Two cautions before anyone quotes off this. The marks disagree by the hour — this paper's own 4:58am tape read $4,276.60 and had silver dead flat, $5.70 and a direction away from the 6:03am bid carried here. And Friday is the event: July non-farm payrolls land at 8:30am, the first full read on American hiring since the Fed held on 29 July with three dissents. June's print was 57,000.

Quote the timestamp with the price this week. Do not reprice a case before Friday morning.

Two thirds of American shoppers have started asking a machine what to buy.

Attentive surveyed 600 US adults online this week. 67% used an AI chatbot — ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity — to help them shop in the past three months, rising to 80% of Gen Z. Among users the common tasks were researching products, comparing brands and features, seeking recommendations and finding deals; 51% used them to compare brands.

The second finding moves the calendar. 62% plan holiday purchases before November and 71% expect to start buying before Black Friday. A jewellery business that treats the season as a five-week sprint from the last Friday in November is now planning into a window where most of the intent has already formed.

Two cautions on the number. A sample of 600 surveyed online skews toward people comfortable answering on a screen — the same population most likely to have tried a chatbot, so 67% is probably a ceiling rather than a floor. And consulting a chatbot is not buying through one; the survey measures consideration, not conversion.

What it does establish is where the consideration happens. Your product copy is now read by a machine before a customer sees it, and a model summarising a page rewards carat weight, metal, setting and price stated plainly. It has nothing to do with an adjective. Write the specification into the page text rather than into an image, and do it before October.

Signet has given its online engagement business to a merchant.

Pam Cloud becomes president of Blue Nile on 10 August, reporting to Joan Hilson, Signet's chief operating and financial officer. She spent more than twenty-five of her thirty years in luxury retail at Tiffany and Co., latterly as senior vice president and chief merchandising officer, and sat on the executive committee. She later founded Roseate Jewelry, a direct-to-consumer pearl brand.

The shape of the hire is the signal. Blue Nile was built on price transparency — sort loose stones by the four Cs, see the number before you walk into a store — and Signet paid $360 million for it in 2022. Putting a Tiffany merchandiser in charge is a decision about assortment, not about traffic. A merchant's instinct is to edit the offer down; a marketplace's is to widen it. The appointment says which one won.

It is the second senior seat filled in a week, and the other went the other way. Pandora named Andre Branch to run North America from 15 August, a marketer with no jewellery background, into a post empty since February. Signet hired depth in the category; Pandora hired breadth outside it. Both presidents start in mid-August, into the same American fourth quarter, which is already substantially bought.

For an independent the useful question is not which is right. It is which one describes your shop — because a business with a distinctive assortment and a business with a distinctive voice need different money spent on them. Neither hire changes anything before November.
